entities.summary:
Antoninus was a Neoplatonist philosopher born around 160 CE in Alexandria, Egypt, to Eustathius and Sosipatra. He dedicated his life to his pupils, establishing a school at Canopus, Egypt, where he spent the remainder of his life, until his death in 400 CE. Although he devoted himself to his pupils, he never expressed an opinion on divine matters, leading some to attribute this to his piety. As an older contemporary of Hypatia, he lived and worked in the shadow of this influential female philosopher. His emphasis on the pursuit of wisdom and his dedication to his pupils reflect his commitment to the Neoplatonist philosophy. Through his teachings, he contributed to the development of this philosophical school, which would go on to influence Western thought. Despite his limited public engagement with divine matters, his philosophical legacy endures, providing valuable insights into the Neoplatonist tradition.

The causes of Antoninus' significance include the cultural and intellectual climate of 4th-century Alexandria, where Neoplatonism flourished, and his role as a mentor to future philosophers, such as Ammonius Hermias. The effects of his influence can be seen in the transmission of Neoplatonist ideas through the works of later philosophers, such as Porphyry and Plotinus. Antoninus' school at Canopus also served as a hub for intellectual inquiry and debate, attracting scholars from across the ancient world.

In terms of relationships, Eunapius' account of Antoninus' piety highlights the complex dynamics between personal devotion and public engagement. The relationship between Antoninus and Hypatia, his contemporary and fellow philosopher, demonstrates the intellectual and personal connections that characterized the ancient world. The places where Antoninus lived and worked include Alexandria, Egypt, and Canopus, Egypt, which served as the site of his school.
